title: Marketing influenced pipeline vs. sourced pipeline, and which one ABM should report
summary: Marketing sourced pipeline judges one campaign. Marketing influenced pipeline, counted by named contact, is the ABM program number. Here's how to report both.
body_markdown:
**Marketing influenced pipeline and marketing sourced pipeline answer two different questions, so an ABM team should report both and put each one on the report where its question gets asked.** Sourced pipeline is the conservative number. It counts the opportunities marketing started, and it's the right way to judge a single campaign or channel. Influenced pipeline counts every opportunity where marketing reached people on the buying committee before the deal opened. Counted by named contact, it's the number for the ABM program, and it's the one that holds up when finance asks what the budget bought.


The argument with finance usually starts when a large influenced number lands on a board slide and nobody can open it. In[our Reality of ABM report (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/guides-and-reports/reality-of-abm-report) , a survey of 239 marketers running live ABM programs, about 40% said they reported $1M or more in marketing-influenced pipeline last quarter. When leadership questions marketing's pipeline contribution, only 15.9% can immediately show evidence everyone in the room agrees on.


## TL;DR


-


Sourced pipeline counts the opportunities marketing started. It's conservative, easy to check, and suited to judging one campaign or channel.


-


Influenced pipeline counts the opportunities where marketing reached the buying committee before the deal opened. ABM works on accounts before they raise a hand, so this is the program number.


-


Influence counted by named contact survives a budget review. Account-level influence ("we touched Acme") is the version finance has learned to discount.


-


Both numbers get gamed in predictable ways. Write the counting rules down before the quarter starts.


-


Put sourced on the campaign report and influenced by named contact on the program report, as two separate lines that never get added together.


## What is marketing sourced pipeline?


Marketing sourced pipeline is the total value of opportunities whose origin was a marketing program. A demo request from a paid search ad or a webinar registrant who becomes an opportunity both start with marketing, and the opportunity carries that origin in its source field.


The calculation is simple, which is most of its appeal:


1. 1


Pick the period and filter opportunities by created date inside it.


2. 2


Keep the ones whose opportunity source, or the original source on the primary contact, is a marketing campaign or channel.


3. 3


Sum the amount, and break it out by campaign and by channel.


Each opportunity has one source, so the number can't double count and it adds up cleanly across campaigns. That makes it the honest way to judge one specific thing. When we turned Google Search into a display campaign, we judged the experiment on[8 demo requests and $36K in sourced pipeline (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/vector-on-vector-an-unhinged-search-as-display-experiment-that-drove-36k-in-pipeline) , because the question was whether that one campaign deserved more budget. The in-platform numbers looked rough. Sourced pipeline told us whether to keep paying for it.


The weakness shows up when you apply it to an ABM program. Sourced pipeline credits whatever started the opportunity, and in an account-based program that's often an SDR's email or a demo request that arrives as direct traffic, with no trace of the campaign that warmed the account up. One respondent in our survey described a 1:1 LinkedIn campaign that reached more than half of an account, followed by an inbound demo request from the same account that came in as direct traffic. Nothing in a sourced report connects the two. Use sourced to decide whether a campaign earns its budget, and expect it to undercount a program built to warm up a buying committee before anyone fills in a form.


## What is marketing influenced pipeline?


Marketing influenced pipeline is the total value of opportunities where marketing reached one or more people on the deal within a fixed window before the opportunity opened. It answers a wider question than sourced: did marketing reach the buyers on this deal before it opened, whoever started it? That's the question an ABM program is built around, because you chose the account before it showed interest and worked on the committee for weeks before sales got a meeting.


The calculation has more decisions in it:


1. 1


List the opportunities created in the period.


2. 2


For each one, pull the contacts on the opportunity and the buying committee mapped to the account.


3. 3


Check whether any of those people had a qualifying marketing touch inside the window, for example the 90 days before the opportunity was created.


4. 4


Count each qualifying opportunity once, at its full amount, however many campaigns touched it.


What counts as a touch, how long the window runs, and when an account counts as reached are decisions you make once, and we've laid them out in[the five decisions behind ABM measurement (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/abm-measurement) . The step that matters here is the last one. Influenced pipeline is a yes or no per opportunity. Once you start splitting a deal's value between the webinar and the retargeting ad, you're building an attribution model, and[attribution models break on account-based programs (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/account-based-marketing-attribution) in ways new weights won't fix.


### What about marketing influenced revenue?


Marketing influenced revenue applies the same rules to closed-won deals. It's the part of influenced pipeline that turned into bookings, and it trails pipeline by a quarter or more. In our survey, 27.6% of teams said they reported $1M or more in influenced revenue. Finance cares about it most and it's the slowest number to read, so put it on the quarterly or annual review and keep influenced pipeline as the leading figure.


## Which influenced pipeline holds up with finance?


Influenced pipeline has a reputation problem, and legacy ABM platforms earned it. Their version counts an opportunity as influenced when anyone at the account's domain saw an ad, or when an account-level engagement score crossed a threshold. That produces a big number fast. It also produces a number nobody can check. Which people? What did they see? Were any of them on the deal? The people drop out before the figure reaches the report, which is the same reason[account-level rollups (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/account-based-marketing-attribution) fail as attribution.


Influenced pipeline by named contact is the version that survives a budget review. It counts an opportunity only when marketing reached an identified person who's on the deal or mapped to a buying role, inside a window you set in advance. Every opportunity in the total then opens to a record: the people on the committee marketing reached, the ads they saw and the pages they visited, the dates, and the deal. A CFO who doubts the figure can pick any opportunity and read it. That's the difference finance cares about. Account-level influence asks them to trust that someone at the account noticed the campaign, while the named-contact version shows them who did and when. The debate then moves to whether those touches mattered, and marketing can answer that with a comparison of reached and unreached accounts.


The survey shows how far most teams are from that record. When leadership questions marketing's contribution, 30.5% say the number holds up only after digging, 25.9% say marketing and sales read the same evidence differently, and 22.2% rebuild the story from scratch. Each of those is an influenced number someone can't open on the spot. When finance pushes back, it's tempting to retreat to sourced pipeline alone, and that hides most of what an ABM program does. Make the influenced number openable and keep it on the report.


## How do sourced and influenced pipeline get gamed?


Both numbers bend under pressure. Sourced pipeline turns into a tug-of-war with sales over a single CRM field, while influenced pipeline tends to grow every quarter whether or not the program improved. Here's where each one goes wrong and the rule that stops it.


### Where sourced pipeline goes wrong


-


**The source field gets overwritten.** If the opportunity source updates to the latest touch, a demo form filled in after three months of SDR work becomes marketing sourced, and sales stops trusting the report. Lock the original source when the opportunity is created.


-


**Bottom-of-funnel channels collect the credit.** Branded search and the demo form sit right before the opportunity, so they look like the best channels on a sourced report. They often catch demand other programs created. Read sourced pipeline by campaign, and don't use it alone to cut upper-funnel spend.


-


**ABM programs look empty.** A program that warms a committee for a quarter and then hands the account to sales sources very little. Judge it on the program report below.


### Where influenced pipeline goes wrong


-


**The window keeps growing.** A 365-day window turns most of your pipeline into influenced pipeline. Set the window before the quarter starts (90 days is a common default for mid-market cycles) and print it on the report.


-


**Any touch counts.** An unopened newsletter or an impression served to someone who isn't on the deal shouldn't qualify. Write down which touches count before you measure anything.


-


**Anyone at the account counts.** That's the account-level version again. Require the touch to land on a named person who's on the opportunity or mapped to a buying role.


-


**Campaigns add up to more than the whole.** When five campaigns each claim the same $200K deal, campaign-level influenced totals sum past total pipeline. Count each opportunity once in the program total, and label campaign-level influence as participation.


-


**Open deals get counted as new.** An opportunity that was already open when the touch happened is acceleration. Report it on its own line.


Sales will challenge both numbers. Rules written down before the quarter are what settle the challenge, because nobody picked them to make this quarter look good.


## Which number goes on which report?


Each report has a reader and a question. Match the number to the question and most of the argument with finance goes away.


-


**Campaign and channel review.** Reader: the marketing team, weekly or monthly. Question: should this campaign get more budget? Number: sourced pipeline by campaign, with influenced participation as context. A result like $36K in sourced pipeline belongs here.


-


**ABM program review.** Reader: marketing leadership and finance, quarterly. Question: what did the program produce? Number: influenced pipeline by named contact, next to a comparison of accounts the program reached against similar accounts it didn't. Show sourced pipeline beside it as the conservative floor.


-


**Board or budget slide.** Reader: the CFO and the exec team. Question: what did the spend buy? Number: influenced pipeline by named contact as the headline, sourced pipeline as the floor under it, influenced revenue once deals have closed, and a note on the window you used.


Never add sourced and influenced pipeline together. In most setups every sourced opportunity also counts as influenced, so the sum double counts the deals marketing started. Report them as two lines and label each one.


Showing both also answers what ABM teams say they want from reporting. In our survey, 23.8% said the outcome they'd most want is a clear picture of what sales and marketing each contributed to a win. Sourced pipeline shows the deals marketing started. The influenced line adds the deals sales opened where marketing had already reached people on the committee, with their names attached, and nobody has to give up credit for either. For the cadence of each report, see[what goes in the weekly, monthly, and quarterly ABM report (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/abm-reporting) . For who owns which number, see[ABM metrics for marketing, sales, and finance (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/abm-success-metrics) .


## What to bring to the next budget review


Bring two numbers and the rules behind them. Sourced pipeline shows finance which campaigns paid for themselves, and it rarely starts an argument because it's conservative. Next to it, influenced pipeline by named contact covers everything the ABM program reached, and because any deal in it opens to a name, a date, and a touch, the larger number holds up too. Put the window and the touch list on the slide, and leave off any number you can't open.

## Frequently asked questions


### What is the difference between marketing sourced and marketing influenced pipeline?


Marketing sourced pipeline counts opportunities whose origin was a marketing program, so each deal has one source and the total adds up cleanly across campaigns. Marketing influenced pipeline counts every opportunity where marketing reached people on the deal within a set window before it opened, including deals sales started. Sourced suits judging a single campaign or channel, and influenced suits judging an ABM program.


### How do you calculate marketing influenced pipeline?


List the opportunities created in the period, pull the contacts on each one and the buying committee mapped to the account, and check whether any of them had a qualifying marketing touch in a fixed window, such as the 90 days before the opportunity was created. Count each qualifying opportunity once at its full amount, however many campaigns touched it. Set the window and the list of qualifying touches before the quarter starts.


### What is marketing influenced revenue?


Marketing influenced revenue is the closed-won part of influenced pipeline: deals where marketing reached people on the buying committee before the opportunity opened and the deal was won. It trails pipeline by a quarter or more, so it belongs on the quarterly or annual review while influenced pipeline serves as the leading figure.


### Should ABM teams report sourced or influenced pipeline?


Report both, on different reports. Sourced pipeline is the conservative number for deciding whether a campaign or channel earns more budget. Influenced pipeline counted by named contact is the number for the ABM program, because the program works on accounts before they raise a hand, and finance can open any deal in it to see who marketing reached and when.


### Can you add sourced and influenced pipeline together?


No. In most setups every sourced opportunity also counts as influenced, so adding them double counts the deals marketing started. Report them as two separate lines, with sourced as the floor and influenced by named contact as the program figure.
